intro: You've searched for a listed building architect near you, so you're likely planning work on a historic property and need someone who understands the extra care that listed buildings demand. Whether it's a repair, an extension or a change of use, you'll want a professional who can guide you through listed building consent and the heritage considerations involved. iComply introduces you to a suitable UK architect who can quote you directly, with fees on application.
need_heading: What people searching for a listed building architect usually need
need_lead: Most people in your position need practical help to alter or maintain a listed building without falling foul of the rules.
needs: You own or are buying a listed property and want to make changes such as a new kitchen, bathroom or extension, but you're unsure what needs listed building consent.
You've been told that repairs are needed to the roof, windows or brickwork, and you want an architect who understands traditional materials and methods.
You're planning to convert a listed building to a new use, such as a home or a business premises, and need help with the planning and heritage aspects.
You've had a previous application refused or faced enforcement action for unauthorised works, and you need expert guidance to put things right.
You want to find a local architect who has experience with the specific type of listed building you own, whether it's a cottage, a farmhouse or a former chapel.
context_heading: One key thing to understand about listed building work
context: Unauthorised works to a listed building are a criminal offence, so it's essential to get the right consent before you start. A listed building architect understands historic fabric and can prepare the heritage statement that is often required to support your application. They will also advise on using traditional materials, which is often important for preserving the building's character.

"Architect" is a protected title in the UK. Only people on the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register can call themselves architects, and they must follow the ARB code of conduct and hold professional indemnity insurance. Many practices are also RIBA Chartered Practices. Architectural designers and technologists can do excellent work too, but they are not registered architects, so it is worth knowing which you are hiring.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the listed building: its grade, its age and style, and its current use, so we can introduce you to an architect with relevant experience.
Explain what you want to do, whether it's a repair, an alteration, an extension or a change of use, and whether you already have any plans or drawings.
Mention any previous applications, consents or enforcement notices, as this will help the architect understand the history.
Say whether the property is in a conservation area or has any other designations, such as being within a national park.
Let us know your rough budget and timescale, even if you're not sure yet, so the architect can tailor their quote.
Confirm your location, as you searched for an architect near you, and we will look for someone who works in your area.
questions: Are you a registered architect with the Architects Registration Board, and can you provide your registration number?
What experience do you have with listed buildings of a similar age and type to mine?
Will you handle the listed building consent application and prepare the heritage statement on my behalf?
How will you approach the use of traditional materials and methods in the work?

faqs.q: Do I always need listed building consent for work on a listed building?
faqs.a: Not all work requires consent, but any alteration that affects the character of the building as a building of special architectural or historic interest will need it. It's always best to check with your local planning authority before starting work, as unauthorised works are a criminal offence.

faqs.q: What is a heritage statement and why is it needed?
faqs.a: A heritage statement is a document that describes the significance of the listed building and assesses the impact of your proposed works. It is often required to support a listed building consent application, and an architect experienced with historic buildings can prepare it for you.

faqs.q: Can I use modern materials on a listed building?
faqs.a: Traditional materials are often important for preserving the character and fabric of a listed building, and using modern materials can sometimes cause damage. Your architect can advise on the most appropriate materials for your specific project and help you understand what the local authority is likely to accept.

faqs.q: How do I check if someone is a registered architect?
faqs.a: You can check the Architects Registration Board (ARB) register online to confirm that someone is a registered architect. Only those on the register can call themselves architects, and they must follow the ARB code of conduct and hold professional indemnity insurance.
